title: Air
intro: Bad air comes in three forms: wildfire smoke that lasts for days, a chemical release that lasts for hours and, rarely, radiation. Each one needs a different room and a different response, so this module keeps them apart. Most of it costs little and is decided before the day you need it.

actions.title: Learn the air quality index and save where to check it
actions.why: Smoke can make the air unhealthy before it looks or smells bad, and the index is what tells you when to act.
actions.how: Open AirNow.gov (or your country's official air quality site), enter your ZIP code and save the page to your phone's home screen. The index runs from 0 to 500: 0 to 50 is good, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy and above 300 hazardous. A simple household rule built on those bands: at 101 or more, anyone at higher risk cuts time outdoors and uses the clean room; at 151 or more, everyone does.
actions.done: The air quality page for your ZIP code opens from an icon on your phone's home screen.

actions.title: Pick your clean room
actions.why: One closed room with filtered air is far easier to keep clean than a whole home.
actions.how: Choose a room big enough for everyone to sleep in, with as few windows and outside doors as possible; a bedroom is the usual choice. On smoke days keep its windows and door shut and run an air cleaner in it: a HEPA cleaner (AR-03), which can run all night, or a box-fan filter (AR-04), which runs only while someone is awake. If it has a window or wall air conditioner, close the outdoor-air damper or set it to recirculate. If the room gets too hot to stay in, heat comes first (AR-07).
actions.done: Everyone at home has been told which room is the clean room and can point to it.
actions.apartment: Smoke also drifts in from the hallway, so choose a room away from your front door if you can.

actions.title: Run a HEPA air cleaner sized for the clean room
actions.why: A portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter removes the fine smoke particles that do the harm.
actions.how: Measure the clean room's floor area and buy a cleaner whose smoke CADR (clean air delivery rate, printed on the box) is big enough for it: EPA's chart asks for at least 65 for 100 sq ft, 130 for 200 sq ft and 390 for 600 sq ft, with an 8-foot ceiling; choose higher for a higher ceiling. Do not buy an ozone generator or any cleaner that makes ozone, which irritates the lungs. On smoke days run it on the highest setting you can live with, day and night, with the room closed. Keep one spare filter, and remember that it stops in an outage unless you have a battery station big enough to run it.
actions.done: An air cleaner whose smoke CADR on the box covers the clean room's floor area is in that room, it switches on, and one spare filter is beside it.

actions.title: Build a box-fan filter if a HEPA cleaner is out of reach
actions.why: A box fan with a furnace filter taped to it cuts indoor smoke for a fraction of the price of a HEPA cleaner.
actions.how: Use a MERV 13 filter that fits a 20-inch box fan: tape it to the back (intake side) with the airflow arrow on the filter frame pointing toward the fan, and seal the edges with tape. Plug the fan straight into the wall with no extension cord, and do not leave children alone with it. CDC says never to leave a home-made unit running unattended. EPA says to use only a 2012-or-later fan with a UL or ETL mark, and that an older fan must never run unattended or while you sleep. This site's rule: run it only while someone is awake in the home. Check the filter every day during smoke, and change it when it turns dark brown or gray or smells of smoke. Treat it as a stand-in for when a tested air cleaner is unavailable or unaffordable: for the night the clean room needs a HEPA cleaner (AR-03). Keep a working smoke alarm in the home.
actions.done: The box-fan filter is built the way this action describes and moves air when you switch it on.

actions.title: Keep N95 respirators for everyone who can wear one
actions.why: A well-fitted N95 filters fine smoke particles, which cloth and surgical masks do not.
actions.how: Buy NIOSH-approved N95s: the mask itself is printed with 'NIOSH' and an approval number starting 'TC-84A', and it almost always has two head straps, not ear loops. Keep 6 for each person who can wear one: that is this site's assumption of 2 a day for 3 smoky days, not an official figure. Then try one on now: pinch the nose clip and check that no air leaks at the edges, which a beard will cause. NIOSH Approved respirators do not come in sizes for very young children, so a young child's protection is the clean room and less time outdoors (AR-17). Anyone with a heart or lung condition should ask their doctor before relying on one. N95s do not stop gases or chemical vapors. Keep them sealed in a bag with your supplies.
actions.done: NIOSH-approved N95s for each person who can wear one are at home, and each of those people has tried one on and checked the edges for leaks.

actions.title: Keep smoke out and do not make more indoors
actions.why: On a smoke day the particles you breathe indoors either leak in from outside or are made by what you do inside.
actions.how: Close all windows and outside doors, and set any air conditioner to recirculate or close its fresh-air intake. If you have a central heating and cooling system, put in a MERV 13 filter, or the highest rating its fan and filter slot can take, and set the fan to On instead of Auto while the air is bad. If the central system has no recirculate setting and no intake you can close, it pulls smoke in: lean on the clean room and its air cleaner (AR-02, AR-03). This site's suggestion: keep that system running for cooling only if the home would otherwise get too hot, because heat comes first (AR-07). Do not fry or broil food, burn candles or incense, smoke, or use a gas stove, and do not vacuum unless the vacuum has a HEPA filter. Use a single-hose portable air conditioner sparingly on smoke days, because it can pull smoke into the room. When the air quality index improves, even for a while, open up and air the home out.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard what to close and what not to do indoors on a smoke day, and any central system holds a MERV 13 filter or the highest rating it takes.

actions.title: Deal with heat first when heat and smoke come together
actions.why: For most people overheating is the more immediate danger of the two, so a closed-up room that gets too hot is the wrong trade.
actions.how: Keep a thermometer in the clean room and watch it. If you cannot hold the room below about 88 °F (31 °C) with the windows shut, or anyone shows signs of heat illness, open the windows for cooler air or go to an air-conditioned place with filtered air, such as a library, mall or cooling center. Wear an N95 on the way if you can wear one. Close up again once the room has cooled. The 88 °F figure is not a promise that the room is safe until then: with a baby, follow FN-05, which does not wait for a number.
actions.done: A thermometer is in the clean room where everyone can read it, and everyone at home can name the air-conditioned place you would go to.

actions.title: Plan how small children get through smoke days
actions.why: NIOSH Approved respirators do not come in sizes for very young children, so a small child's protection has to come from the room and not from a mask.
actions.how: On smoke days keep children indoors, in the clean room (AR-02) with the air cleaner running (AR-03), and plan indoor play for them there. Never put a mask or respirator on a child under 2. CDC says children aged 2 and over can wear a respirator or mask in a size that fits over the nose and under the chin without blocking their sight, and that smaller sizes may not have been designed or tested for children. EPA says not to rely on masks to protect children from smoke. This site follows EPA, the stricter of the two: a mask is for a short trip outside that cannot be avoided, never a reason to go out. If a child has asthma, keep their medicines stocked and with the bag, and get medical help for any new or worsening symptoms. Decide now where you would go for cleaner air (X2-03): CDC says to think about leaving if a child has trouble breathing or other symptoms that do not get better.
actions.done: The clean room has an air cleaner and things for the children to do in it, and the place you would take them for cleaner air is written on your evacuation plan sheet.

actions.title: Learn the shelter-in-place steps for a chemical release
actions.why: After a chemical spill or fire nearby, officials may tell you to stay inside and seal a room rather than go out into contaminated air.
actions.how: When officials say to shelter in place, bring everyone and any pets indoors, lock every window and outside door, turn off fans, air conditioning and heating, and close any fireplace damper. Take medicines, phones and chargers to your prepared room (AR-09) and shut the door. Tape plastic sheeting over its windows, close and tape the vents, and tape around the door; if you have no plastic, stuff towels, sheets or clothing into the vents and under the door. Follow a radio or news app and stay until officials give the all clear or tell you to leave; a sealed room is for a few hours (AR-11 has the air limit). Do not use this room choice for radiation: there the safe place is the center or basement of the building (AR-12).
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the shelter-in-place steps read aloud and can point to the room you would go to.

actions.title: Choose and prepare your seal-up room
actions.why: Sealing a room takes minutes when the plastic is already cut and far too long when it is not.
actions.how: Pick a room with at least 10 square feet of floor for each person, on the highest floor you can, with as few windows as possible and a water source if you can (a bedroom with its own bathroom works well), that you can seal off from outside air. Measure each window, door and vent, cut plastic sheeting 4 mil or thicker a few inches wider all around, and label each piece by window. Store the pieces in that room with duct tape, scissors, towels, a battery radio and drinking water. Practice once by finding every vent, exhaust fan and window air conditioner you would need to cover. A sealed room is for a few hours (AR-11 has the air limit).
actions.done: The cut, labeled plastic is stored in the room with tape, scissors, towels, a battery radio and water, and you have done the practice round of its vents.
actions.apartment: Note any bathroom or kitchen exhaust fan, dryer vent or vent grille, because each needs covering too, and do not choose a basement or garage level. In a building with shared ventilation, sealing your own room is only part of the job; ask management how the system is shut down (see AR-10).

actions.title: Ask how your building's ventilation is shut down
actions.why: In many apartment buildings, fans that residents do not control push outdoor air into the hallways and units.
actions.how: Ask management three things: does the building bring outdoor air into hallways or units, who can switch that off in an emergency, and how will residents be told. Then list what you control yourself: bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans, any window or through-wall air conditioner, a fresh-air vent, the thermostat's fan setting. Write the answers by hand on the printable Building information sheet and keep it with your plan.
actions.done: Management's answers to the three questions and the list of what you control yourself are written on the Building information sheet.

actions.title: Know how long a sealed room is good for
actions.why: A taped room holds only the air that was in it when you sealed it, so it protects you for a few hours and is not a place to live.
actions.how: Use a room with at least 10 square feet of floor for each person; FEMA's figure is that this gives enough air for up to 5 hours at rest. Take water, medicines, phones, chargers and the radio in with you. Most chemical clouds thin out within a few hours, and officials decide when you leave: keep the radio or your alerts on and follow them, including an order to evacuate. An order to stay indoors for longer, which CDC says can last days, means windows shut and ventilation off, not living in the taped room. When officials give the all clear, take down the plastic, open the windows and vents and air the home out.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard this action read aloud and can say who decides when you leave the sealed room.

actions.title: Learn the opposite room rule for radiation
actions.why: Against radioactive fallout it is thick walls and distance from the roof and outer walls that protect you, not a sealed room.
actions.how: If you are told of a radiation emergency or a nuclear explosion, get inside the nearest solid building at once and go to the basement or the middle of the building, away from windows, outer walls and the roof; in a tall building, an inside hallway or stairwell away from the roof and outer walls. Stay inside for 24 hours unless officials say otherwise, with windows shut and ventilation off, and do not go out to collect family, who should shelter where they are. If you were outdoors, take off your outer clothes at the door, bag them, and wash or wipe exposed skin and hair. Plastic sheeting gives no shielding, so this is not the chemical-release room (AR-08), which is chosen for height above ground and few openings.
actions.done: Everyone at home can point to the place in your building you would shelter in for a radiation emergency.

actions.title: If you live within 10 miles of a nuclear power plant, get potassium iodide the official way
actions.why: Potassium iodide taken when officials say to keeps radioactive iodine out of the thyroid gland, which matters most for babies, children and anyone pregnant or breastfeeding, and it protects against nothing else.
actions.how: Check on your state emergency management or health department website whether your address is inside a nuclear plant's 10-mile emergency planning zone, and how your state gives out potassium iodide. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission supplies tablets to states that ask for them for people inside that zone, and each state decides how they reach you. If your state offers them, get them that way, keep them in their package with your medicines, store them as the package says, and note the expiration date printed on it. Take or give them only when public health or emergency officials say to, never in advance. The dose depends on age, and tablets come in different strengths, so follow the leaflet in the box you own and your state's own instructions; taking more, or more often, gives no more protection and can cause severe illness or death. Anyone with an iodine sensitivity, a thyroid condition or any other health concern should ask their doctor now whether they can take it. The tablets add to leaving or sheltering when you are told to and do not replace either (AR-12). If you are outside the zone, skip this action.
actions.done: Your state's website shows whether your address is inside a plant's 10-mile zone and, if it is and your state gives out tablets, the package is with your medicines.

actions.title: Copy your area, sirens, stations and reception center from the plant's emergency booklet
actions.why: Homes inside a nuclear plant's 10-mile emergency planning zone are sent emergency information regularly, and it holds the details for your address that no general page can give.
actions.how: If you live within 10 miles of a nuclear power plant, find the emergency information sent to homes in its emergency planning zone: it may come as a booklet, a wall calendar, a flyer or a notice with a utility bill, and your county or state emergency management office can tell you where to get it. Copy onto your evacuation plan sheet what it gives for your address: your area or zone, how you will be warned (sirens or other alerts) and what to do when you hear them, the radio and TV stations to tune to, your evacuation route, and the reception center where people who leave are checked for radiation. Keep the booklet with your plan, and copy the new details when a new one arrives. Potassium iodide is in AR-18 and sheltering in AR-12. If you are outside the zone, skip this action.
actions.done: Your area or zone, the warning signal, the stations, the route and the reception center are written on your evacuation plan sheet, and the booklet is kept with your plan.

actions.title: Know what to do if you smell gas
actions.why: Leaking gas can be set off by a spark as small as the one inside a light switch.
actions.how: If you smell gas or hear hissing, get everyone out at once. Touch no switches, appliances or phones on the way, and do not stop to find or turn a valve. Do not go back in. From a safe distance call the gas utility's emergency number or 911. Only the utility turns the gas back on. Carbon monoxide is a different gas with no smell at all, and only an alarm detects it.
actions.done: Everyone at home has heard the steps for a gas smell read aloud once.
actions.apartment: Take the stairs, not the elevator, and do not go looking for the building's gas valve; that is for management and the utility, so tell management once you are out.
actions.cite_todo: No source opened covers the elevator; the stairs line is this site's reading of the rule against touching anything electrical on the way out.

actions.title: Keep dust protection for after a collapse or earthquake
actions.why: A damaged building fills the air with fine dust from concrete, plaster and glass that harms lungs and eyes.
actions.how: For each person who can wear them, keep one of your N95s (AR-05) and one pair of close-fitting safety goggles beside the bed with the shoes and light, and another set in each grab bag. Put them on before you move through dust or clear debris; with neither on hand, breathe through a tightly woven cotton cloth. An N95 filters dust only, not gas or chemical vapor, so if you smell gas, leave (AR-13).
actions.done: For each person who can wear them, an N95 and a pair of goggles are beside the bed with the shoes and light, and another set is in each grab bag.

actions.title: Protect people at higher risk from smoke first
actions.why: Smoke harms some people sooner and at lower levels: those with heart or lung disease, older adults, babies and children, and anyone who is pregnant.
actions.how: If someone in your home is in one of those groups, the clean room and the air cleaner are theirs first, from the moment the index passes 100. Before smoke season, ask their doctor what to do on smoke days and keep rescue inhalers and other medicines stocked. Agree in advance where they would go for cleaner air if coughing, wheezing or chest tightness starts, and call 911 for chest pain or severe trouble breathing.
actions.done: Anyone at higher risk has asked their doctor about smoke days, their medicines are stocked, and everyone at home has agreed where they would go for cleaner air.

actions.title: Make a plan for an illness that spreads at home
actions.why: When one person catches something that spreads through the air, a few habits can keep the rest of a small home well.
actions.how: Decide which room the sick person would stay in with the door closed, and how the bathroom would be shared and wiped down. Keep a box with N95s for the sick person and the caregiver, soap, hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, disposable gloves and a household disinfectant. Never put a mask or respirator on a child under 2, or on anyone who cannot take it off themselves. Open a window in the sick room when the outdoor air is good, or run the air cleaner there, and wipe shared handles, faucets and switches every day. Follow current public health advice on how long to stay apart.
actions.done: The box is packed with everything this action lists, and everyone at home has been told which room a sick person would stay in.
